label: Demand rises and supply falls with height together, so the flyable heights reach down to the ground
statement_en: In an atmosphere where air density and oxygen partial pressure both fall with height, the minimum speed of lift-supported flight and the power to fly at it are nondecreasing in height, while the aerobic supply (with arterial content nondecreasing in partial pressure, as a Hill curve gives) is nonincreasing. Hence sustained flight possible at a height is possible at every lower height; above an infeasible height every height is infeasible, so the flyable set is an interval from the ground up to a ceiling; and a design that cannot fly at the ground cannot fly at any height. A larger lifting area lowers the power required at a fixed height.

hypotheses.name: altitude-coupling#assumed-1
hypotheses.statement: A monotone atmosphere: both density and oxygen partial pressure fall with height. No profile, no numbers; the candidates' profile is the physics thread's NASA Glenn fit.

hypotheses.name: altitude-coupling#assumed-2
hypotheses.statement: Arterial content nondecreasing in partial pressure (a Hill curve is, but the Hill equation, the Bohr shift and the Root effect are not formalised).

hypotheses.name: altitude-coupling#assumed-3
hypotheses.statement: Everything else held fixed with height: the animal makes no compensation (haematocrit, ventilation, cardiac output), and temperature, humidity and wind are outside the model.

hypotheses.name: altitude-coupling#assumed-4
hypotheses.statement: The size of the effect is NOT proved: it is gentle, and the binding constraint for the real fish is the aerobic ceiling at sea level.

scope.basis: a theorem about a model: it applies wherever the design supplies the quantities it uses and accepts the hypotheses in scope.assumed
kernelChecked: That the minimum speed and the power required at it are nondecreasing in height, given only that air density falls with height.
That the aerobic supply is nonincreasing in height, given only that oxygen partial pressure falls with height and arterial content is nondecreasing in it.
That the feasible heights are downward closed, that infeasibility propagates upward (a ceiling in that sense), and that infeasibility at the ground forces infeasibility everywhere.
That a larger lifting area lowers the power required at a fixed height.
assumed: A monotone atmosphere: both density and oxygen partial pressure fall with height. No profile, no numbers; the candidates' profile is the physics thread's NASA Glenn fit.
Arterial content nondecreasing in partial pressure (a Hill curve is, but the Hill equation, the Bohr shift and the Root effect are not formalised).
Everything else held fixed with height: the animal makes no compensation (haematocrit, ventilation, cardiac output), and temperature, humidity and wind are outside the model.
The size of the effect is NOT proved: it is gentle, and the binding constraint for the real fish is the aerobic ceiling at sea level.
